title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: The waiting room of the celebrated Petersburg lawyer was full when Alexey Alexandrovitch walked in. Three women — an elderly lady, a young one, and a merchant's wife — and three men — a German banker with a ring on his finger, a bearded merchant, and a furious-looking government clerk in official uniform with a cross at his neck — had clearly been waiting a long while already. Two clerks sat at tables scratching away with their pens. The fittings on the writing tables, of which Alexey Alexandrovitch himself was very particular, were unusually fine. He noticed it in spite of himself. One of the clerks, without standing up, turned on him with a half-closed glare. "What is it you want?"
He answered that he had come to see the lawyer on a matter of business.
"He's busy," the clerk said curtly, and pointed his pen at the people waiting before going back to his writing.
"Could he not spare me a moment?" Alexey Alexandrovitch asked.
"He has no free time — he is always busy. Kindly take your turn."
"Then I must trouble you to take in my card," Alexey Alexandrovitch said with dignity, realizing there was no way to remain anonymous.
The clerk took the card and, plainly not pleased by what he read, went off to the inner door.

Alexey Alexandrovitch was in principle a supporter of open legal proceedings, though for certain higher official reasons he disliked the way the principle was applied in Russia and disapproved of it — as far as one could disapprove of anything established by authority of the Emperor. His entire career had been spent in administration, and so, whenever he found fault with something, his disapproval was always softened by the awareness that mistakes were inevitable and that reform was possible in every department. In the new public courts he disliked the restrictions placed on the lawyers conducting cases. But until now he had had no personal contact with the courts, and his disapproval of their openness had been purely theoretical; now it was reinforced by the disagreeable impression made on him by the lawyer's waiting room.
"He'll be with you in a moment," the clerk said; and two minutes later the bulky figure of an old solicitor who had been consulting with the lawyer did indeed appear in the doorway.

The lawyer was a short, squat, bald man with a dark reddish beard, long pale eyebrows, and a heavy overhanging brow. He was dressed as though for a wedding — from his cravat down to his double watch chain and his polished boots. His face was shrewd and manly, but his clothes were dandyish and in poor taste.
"Please come in," the lawyer said, addressing Alexey Alexandrovitch, and ushered him gloomily ahead before closing the door.

"Won't you sit down?" He gestured to an armchair beside a writing table piled with papers. He sat down himself and, rubbing his small short-fingered hands — the backs of them covered with white hairs — tilted his head to one side. He had barely settled into that posture when a moth flew across the table. With a quickness no one would have guessed at, the lawyer flung out his hands, caught the moth, and resumed his position.

"Before I go into my business," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, watching the lawyer's movements with astonished eyes, "I should mention that the matter I have to speak about must be kept strictly private."
The lawyer's heavy reddish mustache parted in a barely perceptible smile.
"I should not be a lawyer if I couldn't keep the secrets entrusted to me. But if you would like assurance...."
Alexey Alexandrovitch glanced at his face and saw that the shrewd gray eyes were laughing — and looked as though they already knew the whole story.
"You know my name?" Alexey Alexandrovitch went on.
"I know you and the fine" — he caught another moth — "work you do, like every Russian," said the lawyer, bowing.
Alexey Alexandrovitch drew a breath and steadied himself. But once he had decided, he went on in his shrill voice, without timidity or hesitation, putting weight on a word here and there.

"I have had the misfortune," Alexey Alexandrovitch began, "to be deceived in my marriage, and I wish to end all ties with my wife by legal means — that is, by divorce — but in such a way that my son will not remain with his mother."

The lawyer's gray eyes did their best not to laugh, but they were dancing with irrepressible glee, and Alexey Alexandrovitch saw it was not simply the satisfaction of a man who had landed a profitable case: there was triumph and elation in them, a gleam like the malicious glint he had seen in his wife's eyes.
"You wish my help in obtaining a divorce?"

"Yes, precisely; but I must warn you that I may be wasting your time and attention. I have come only to consult you as a first step. I want a divorce, but the form in which it can be obtained is of great importance to me. It's quite possible that if that form does not suit my requirements, I will give up the idea of a legal divorce."
"Oh, that's always how it is," the lawyer said, "and that is always for you to decide."

He let his eyes drop to Alexey Alexandrovitch's feet, feeling he might give offense if his client caught sight of the amusement he could not suppress. A moth fluttered past his nose; he twitched his hands but held back from catching it out of respect for Alexey Alexandrovitch's situation.

"Although the general outlines of our laws on this subject are known to me," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on, "I should be glad to have some sense of the forms in which such things are handled in practice."

"You would be glad," the lawyer answered, eyes still down, taking up his client's manner of speech with a certain satisfaction, "for me to set out for you all the means by which you could achieve what you want?"
And on receiving a confirming nod from Alexey Alexandrovitch, he went on, stealing a glance now and then at the face opposite him, which was turning red in patches.

"Under our laws," he said, with a faint hint of disapproval of those laws, "divorce is possible, as you know, in the following cases.... One moment!" he called to a clerk who poked his head in at the door; nevertheless he got up, exchanged a few words with him, and sat down again. "... In the following cases: physical defect in one of the parties, desertion without communication for five years" — he crooked one short hair-covered finger — "adultery" (this word he pronounced with evident relish), "subdivided as follows" (he continued crooking his plump fingers, though plainly the three cases and their subdivisions could not really be put on the same footing): "physical defect of the husband or of the wife, adultery of the husband or of the wife." Since by now he had used up all his fingers, he straightened them out again and went on: "That is the theory; but I imagine you have done me the honor of coming to me to find out how it works in practice. Therefore, going on precedent, I must tell you that in practice every divorce case can be reduced to the following — no physical defect, I take it, and no desertion either?..."
Alexey Alexandrovitch bowed his head in agreement.

"— reduces, then, to this: adultery on the part of one spouse, and detection of the guilty party in the act, either by mutual arrangement or, failing such arrangement, by accident. It must be said that the second of those is rarely seen in practice," the lawyer remarked, and shooting a glance at Alexey Alexandrovitch, paused — like a man selling pistols who has finished praising each one and is now waiting for the customer to choose. But Alexey Alexandrovitch said nothing, so the lawyer continued: "The most usual and straightforward course — the sensible one, in my view — is adultery by mutual consent. I would not allow myself to put it that way to an uneducated client," he said, "but I assume you take my meaning."
Alexey Alexandrovitch was so shaken, however, that he did not at once grasp the good sense of adultery by mutual consent, and his eyes betrayed his confusion; the lawyer was quick to assist him.

"People cannot go on living together — that is the fact. And if both of them agree on the point, the details and formalities don't matter much. At the same time it is the simplest and most reliable method."
Alexey Alexandrovitch now understood completely. But he had religious scruples that stood in the way of such a plan.
"That is out of the question in my case," he said. "Only one option remains: accidental detection, supported by letters which I have in my possession."
At the mention of letters the lawyer pursed his lips and produced a thin little sound of compassion and contempt.

"Consider, please," he began, "that cases of that sort, as you know, fall under ecclesiastical jurisdiction; the reverend fathers are fond of going into the smallest details in such cases," he said with a smile that revealed his sympathy with the reverend fathers' taste. "Letters may, of course, provide partial confirmation; but the detection must be of the most direct kind — that is, by eyewitnesses. In fact, if you do me the honor of placing your confidence in me, you will do well to leave the choice of methods to me. If you want the result, you must accept the means."
"If that is so...." Alexey Alexandrovitch began, suddenly going pale; but at that moment the lawyer got up and went to the door again to deal with the intruding clerk.
"Tell her we don't haggle over our fees!" he said, and came back to Alexey Alexandrovitch.
On his way back he caught yet another moth without being noticed. "My rep curtains will be in a fine state by the summer!" he thought, frowning.
"You were saying?..." he prompted.

"I will let you know my decision by letter," Alexey Alexandrovitch said, standing up and gripping the table. He stood for a moment in silence, then said: "From what you have told me I may, therefore, conclude that a divorce can be obtained? I would ask you to let me know your terms."

"It can be obtained if you give me complete freedom of action," the lawyer answered, ignoring his question. "When may I expect to hear from you?" he asked, moving toward the door, his eyes and his polished boots gleaming.
"In a week. Please be so kind as to send me your reply as to whether you will take the case, and on what terms."
"Very good."

The lawyer bowed respectfully, saw his client out, and, left alone, gave himself up to his amusement. He felt so cheerful that, against his usual rules, he made a reduction in his terms for the haggling lady, and gave up catching moths, having decided once and for all that next winter he must have the furniture reupholstered in velvet, like Sigonin's.
